justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias with relatively flat expected drift over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 141.5 likely anchored closely to the most recent observed price, with a small directional lean based on prevailing momentum signals, recent volume patterns, or short-term technical levels. At one week, the slight upward nudge to 142.0 reflects a continuation assumption — that whatever trend was in place would persist with modest positive drift, consistent with the broader market environment at the time. At one month, the 143.0 estimate represents a longer-run mean reversion or trend extrapolation, essentially assuming the asset continues grinding higher at a moderate pace while acknowledging that the compounding of daily uncertainties makes any specific endpoint less reliable.

The confidence interval widths grow substantially as the horizon extends, which is the natural consequence of uncertainty accumulating over time. At one day, the 90% CI of roughly 6.6 points wide reflects typical intraday-to-overnight volatility for an asset in this price range. By one week, the interval widens to 13 points, capturing the possibility of macro data releases, earnings, or sentiment shifts. At one month, the 28-point wide interval reflects the full range of plausible outcomes when compounding weekly risks — including policy decisions, sector rotations, and liquidity changes — all of which can materially alter price trajectory.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise deterioration in macroeconomic data, a sharp risk-off event such as a geopolitical shock, or unexpected hawkish central bank communication could push prices well below the lower bounds, especially at the one-month horizon. On the upside, a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices above 157 within the month. Liquidity conditions also matter — if market depth is thin, moves can overshoot fundamental levels more easily.

It is worth noting that these intervals, while wide, still reflect a relatively benign base case. Fat-tail events — a flash crash, a systemic credit event, or an unexpected geopolitical escalation — are not well-captured by symmetric confidence intervals, and true tail risk is likely underrepresented. Consumers of this forecast should treat the outer bounds as probabilistic guideposts rather than hard limits, understanding that roughly 10% of outcomes by construction are expected to fall outside them.
